div.head: 393. Paper Prepared in the Central Intelligence Agency
div.p: Ecuador: The Danger of a Military Coup

Next year promises to be a difficult and crucial period for Ecuador’s strained democracy as balloting to elect its next president is scheduled to begin in January. We anticipate that political infighting between a resurgent left and President Febres-Cordero’s weakened government will escalate soon. Although we judge that the Ecuadorean military would prefer not to take power directly, the Army in particular has become increasingly enmeshed in politics—as Febres-Cordero’s most loyal defense—and therefore has gradually grown more politicized. Recent reporting from the Embassy [less than 1 line not declassified] suggests that top military leaders fear that the left—which they consider subversive and communist—is becoming increasingly powerful and disruptive.

We do not believe a military coup is imminent, chiefly because the majority of senior officers support Febres-Cordero and apparently see him as effective in countering leftist provocations. Frequent political clashes between the left and the government, however,
are a virtual certainty from 10 August 1987 when Congress opens until the next government takes office in August 1988. If the military deems it necessary to step in to defend Febres-Cordero or to restore public order, particularly on a repetitive basis, the potential for a general or a group of senior officers to take power will grow.
[Omitted here is the body of the paper.]

note.p: Source: Central Intelligence Agency, Office of Support Services (DI), Job 90T00114R: Intelligence Publications Files (1986–1987), Box 1, Folder 38: ALA 87–20046, Ecuador: The Danger of a Military Coup.
